title: Compound nouns and -ki
intro: Put two nouns side by side, give the second one `-(s)I`, and you have a compound noun: *Türk kahvesi* (Turkish coffee), *otobüs durağı* (bus stop). This unit shows how compounds take case endings and possessives, when to use the genitive of [A1 unit 10](gp-genitive-possessive) instead, and the suffix `-ki`, which turns a place or a time into an adjective (*masadaki kitap*, the book on the table) or a pronoun (*benimki*, mine).

blocks.text: In the possessive phrase of [A1 unit 10](gp-genitive-possessive), the first noun takes the genitive and points to a particular owner: *evin kapısı* (the door of the house). Leave out the genitive and the first noun stops pointing to anyone: it only says what **kind** of thing the second noun is. *Ev kapısı* is a front door, any front door. This is the compound noun (*belirtisiz isim tamlaması*): a bare noun, then a noun with `-(s)I`.

The `-(s)I` is the third-person possessive of [A1 unit 9](gp-possessive-suffixes), with all its habits: s after a vowel (*kahvesi*), softening of the last consonant (*durak* → *durağı*, *bardak* → *bardağı*), and y after *su*: *portakal suyu*. Here it doesn't mean **his** or **her**: it only ties the two nouns together.

**Case endings after a compound.** The `-(s)I` stays, and an n comes before the case ending, exactly as after any third-person possessive ([A1 unit 10](gp-pronominal-n)). The one exception is `-(y)lA`, which takes y: *Türk kahvesiyle*. The plural comes before the `-(s)I`, which then shrinks to `-I`: *otobüs durakları* (bus stops).

blocks.text: **Compounds written as one word.** Some old compounds have become single words, and they behave the same way: *havalimanı* (airport, from *hava limanı*, air harbour) gives *havalimanına* (to the airport); *zeytinyağı* (olive oil) gives *zeytinyağıyla*. You already know *kahverengi* (brown, coffee-colour) and *ayakkabı* (shoe), once *ayak kabı*, a container for the foot.

**Names.** Many names are compounds: *İstanbul Üniversitesi*, *Ankara Garı*, *Türk Dil Kurumu*. The suffix sits on the common noun, so there is no apostrophe, and names of institutions take none before a case ending either: *İstanbul Üniversitesinde okuyor* (she studies at Istanbul University). Place names alone keep it: *İstanbul'da*.

items.tr: Bir Türk kahvesi ve bir portakal suyu, lütfen.
items.seg: Bir Türk kahve|s|i ve bir portakal su|y|u, lütfen.
items.en: A Turkish coffee and an orange juice, please.
I love lentil soup.
I'm waiting at the bus stop.
We're going to the airport by taxi.
My older sister studies at Istanbul University.
The coffee cups are in the cupboard.

blocks.text: Both parts are needed: *Türk kahve* and *mercimek çorba* are wrong. On menus you will see *Adana kebap* or *İskender kebap* without `-(s)I`; in speech and careful writing, *Adana kebabı*.
A nationality word before a noun is an adjective, not a compound: *Türk öğretmen* is a teacher who is Turkish. A teacher **of** Turkish is a compound with the language: *Türkçe öğretmeni*.
English also lines nouns up, **bus stop**, **orange juice**, but marks neither; French joins them with de: un arrêt de bus. Turkish marks the second noun: *otobüs durağı*.

A compound can belong to someone. The personal possessive then **replaces** the `-(s)I`, because a noun takes only one possessive: *okul çantası* (school bag) → *okul çantam* (my school bag), never *okul çantasım*.

With a noun as owner, put it in the genitive in front of the whole compound, which keeps its `-(s)I`: *Ali'nin okul çantası* (Ali's school bag), *annemin doğum günü* (my mother's birthday). A case ending then follows with its n: *Ali'nin doğum gününde* (at Ali's birthday).
**Genitive or not?** With the genitive, the first noun is a particular owner. Without it, the first noun only names a kind. The same two nouns can do both:

**Compounds inside compounds.** A compound can be the first part of a new one, and in everyday words both keep their `-(s)I`: *doğum günü partisi* (birthday party), *Türk kahvesi fincanı* (a Turkish coffee cup). Some official names drop the inner one: the *Türk Dil Kurumu*, the body behind the spelling rules of this course, although the language itself is *Türk dili*.
**Adjectives go in front of the whole compound**, never between its two nouns: *yeni okul çantam* (my new school bag), *sıcak bir Türk kahvesi* (a hot Turkish coffee).

items.en: Where is my school bag?
My mother's birthday is tomorrow.
We're going to Ali's birthday party.
I can't find my house key.
This is a children's book.
Happy birthday!

blocks.text: *Okul çantasım* and *doğum günüm partisi* are wrong. **My** replaces the `-(s)I` of the compound it belongs to: *okul çantam*; and a compound inside a compound keeps its own: *doğum günü partim* (my birthday party).
*Bir* also goes before the compound, or between an adjective and the compound: *bir Türk kahvesi*, *güzel bir doğum günü partisi*.

sections.title: Masadaki kitap: -ki after places and times

blocks.text: English puts a place after the noun it describes: **the book on the table**. Turkish can't: *kitap masada* is a sentence (the book is on the table). Instead, `-ki` turns the locative *masada* into an adjective, *masadaki* (that is on the table), and like every adjective it goes in front: *masadaki kitap*.

Time words take `-ki` without the locative: *yarınki toplantı* (tomorrow's meeting), *sabahki ders* (this morning's class), *geçen haftaki maç* (last week's match), *şimdiki* (present, current). It also follows the place nouns of [unit 9](gp-place-nouns): *evin önündeki araba* (the car in front of the house).

**-ki doesn't harmonize.** It is *-ki* after back vowels too: *okuldaki*, *odadaki*, *yarınki*. The exceptions are three words: *bugünkü*, *dünkü* and *öbürkü* (the other one). Its k never softens either: *evdekini* (the one at home, as an object).

**Spelling.** The suffix `-ki` is written together with its word: *evdeki*. Don't confuse it with the conjunction *ki*, written apart, which comes in [B2 unit 8](b2-u08), or with the suffix `-DA` and the word *de* of [A1 unit 4](gp-de-also): *evde de* (at home too).

items.en: Is the tea on the table yours?
My friend in Istanbul is coming tomorrow.
Tomorrow's meeting is at ten.
Have you read today's paper?
Yesterday's match was very exciting.
Whose is the car in front of the house?

blocks.text: *Kitap masada* is a sentence: **The book is on the table.** *Masadaki kitap* is only a phrase, **the book on the table**, and still needs a verb: *Masadaki kitap benim.*
English and French put the place after the noun: **the book on the table**, le livre sur la table. Turkish turns it into an adjective and puts it first: *masadaki kitap*.
After a genitive, `-ki` makes a pronoun that stands for a noun already mentioned: *benimki* (mine), *Ali'ninki* (Ali's). *Senin araban kırmızı, benimki mavi* (Your car is red; mine is blue).

These pronouns take the plural and the cases. Before a case ending they add n, as a third-person possessive does: *benimkiler* (mine, several of them), *benimkini* (mine, as a definite object), *seninkinde* (in yours), *Ali'ninkine* (to Ali's).

`-ki` after a locative also makes a pronoun: *masadaki* (the one on the table), *evdekiler* (the people at home), *oradakiler* (the ones over there). And *bizimkiler*, literally **ours**, is the everyday way to say **my family, my folks**.

items.en: Your car is red; mine is blue.
Ali's house is big; Ayşe's is small.
My phone isn't working; can I use yours?
Who are the people over there?
My family is coming this evening.

blocks.text: To say whose something is, the genitive alone is enough: *Bu kitap benim* (This book is mine). Use `-ki` when the noun itself is left out: *Benimki şurada* (Mine is over there).
After `-ki`, the accusative is *-ni*, with the n: *seninkini*, not *seninkiyi*.

summary: A compound noun is a bare noun + a noun with `-(s)I`: *Türk kahvesi*, *otobüs durağı*, *portakal suyu*. It names a kind of thing, not an owner.
Case endings after a compound take an n: *Türk kahvesini*, *otobüs durağında*, *havalimanına*; `-(y)lA` takes y: *kahvesiyle*.
A personal possessive replaces the `-(s)I`: *okul çantam*, never *okul çantasım*. A noun owner goes in front, in the genitive: *Ali'nin okul çantası*.
Genitive for a particular owner (*çocuğun kitabı*), compound for a kind (*çocuk kitabı*).
`-ki` turns a locative or a time word into an adjective that goes before the noun: *masadaki kitap*, *yarınki toplantı*. It doesn't harmonize, except in *bugünkü*, *dünkü*, *öbürkü*.
After a genitive, `-ki` makes a pronoun: *benimki, seninki, Ali'ninki*; with a case ending, an n: *seninkini*.
